USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the March 1 clock running and negotiate hard in the current high-level round without new tariff hikes, new entity-list moves, or any rollback. Take Chinese purchase offers as a down payment, not a deal. Insist that any path off the List 3 10-to-25 percent hike include enforceable commitments on IP, forced tech transfer, and verification—the issues that collapsed the May 2018 truce. Keep the Huawei/Meng criminal process on a separate legal track and do not trade it for a purchase package.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is modestly above neutral, not high and not an opportunity. The US already covers ~$250B of Chinese imports (Lists 1–2 at 25%, List 3 at 10%) and China is at the table, which is leverage. But the original Section 301 complaint is still unmet: the 2019-01-07 and 2019-01-30 rounds discussed purchases while structural IP/tech-transfer and enforcement remained open, and Lighthizer told Ways and Means in mid-January he would not extend the March 1 deadline. That cliff is useful only if it is not fired blindly. Offset: China’s retaliation has already hit a core US export constituency—soy sales to China fell ~94% through mid-October, September US-to-China bean shipments were down >80%, and USDA/ASA documented a ~$2/bushel price break plus $12B in stopgap farm aid. US consumer sentiment dropped from 100.1 to 91.2 and industrial production slipped into January; the 10-year yield fell to 2.70% and the curve flattened, showing markets are pricing slower growth even as VIX cooled from the December 36 spike to 17.66. The 2019-01-28 Huawei/Meng indictments and extradition request, unsealed as Liu He arrived, add a second front Beijing calls political suppression; treating that as a trade chip would either blow up talks or sell out a sanctions/IP case. Escalating tariffs now would likely trigger matching Chinese retaliation and deepen farm and market stress with ~30 days still on the clock. Conceding purchases or a partial rollback would repeat May 19–29 (Mnuchin “on hold,” then the White House reopened 301). Negotiate, hold existing tariffs, and make March 2 the priced alternative if structure and enforcement are not on paper.
key_factors: 90-day G20 truce still in force; List 3 hike to 25% suspended but scheduled if no deal by ~March 1
High-level talks underway (Jan 7 working level; Jan 30 Lighthizer/Mnuchin–Liu He) with purchases discussed and structural IP/tech-transfer/enforcement still unresolved
US already has ~$250B of Section 301 coverage; further tariff escalation is a stored threat, not a needed next step this week
Farm-belt retaliation is the main realized US cost: China 25% soy tariff, ~94% drop in sales, price collapse, $12B aid
Huawei/Meng criminal track (Dec 1 arrest; Jan 28 DOJ charges and extradition) is a live non-tariff shock that US officials say is separate from trade—do not bargain it away
US macro is not in crisis but is softening (sentiment, IP, flattening curve); China health series were unavailable, so do not over-claim opponent distress

sources_cited.excerpt: USTR Section 301 report finds China IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable; Trump directs tariffs, WTO case, and investment restrictions.
Joint statement: China to significantly increase US purchases; Mnuchin says trade war is on hold. Truce collapses 10 days later.
List 3 takes effect at 10%; China retaliates 5–10% on ~$60B; combined US 301 coverage ~$250B.
G20: 90-day negotiation window; planned Jan 1 List 3 hike to 25% suspended. Same day Canada arrests Meng Wanzhou on US request.
Talks resume in Beijing; China discusses increased US purchases; structural issues remain open.
DOJ unseals fraud/sanctions charges against Huawei and Meng; US formally requests extradition from Canada.
Lighthizer and Mnuchin in high-level talks; purchase commitments discussed; enforcement and structural IP/tech-transfer unresolved.
University of Michigan consumer sentiment fell from 100.1 (Sep 2018) to 91.2 (Jan 2019).
US industrial production eased to 103.40 in Jan 2019 from ~104.10 in Sep 2018.
10-year Treasury yield 2.70% on 2019-01-30, down from a ~3.24% November peak; curve flattened vs 2-year at 2.52%.
VIX 17.66 on 2019-01-30 after a December spike to 36.07—stress eased but remains above mid-2018 single digits.
US goods imports from China fell to $41.3B in Jan 2019 from $49.9B in Sep 2018 (−17%).
Lighthizer told Ways and Means the March 1 tariff-escalation deadline would not be extended; Mnuchin/Kudlow stress IP, no forced JVs, and enforcement; USCBC says China has not tabled much new.
Jan 7–9 Beijing talks emphasized purchases and a foundation for later talks; little evidence of progress on structural industrial-policy change; May 2018 purchase deal is the cautionary precedent.
DOJ unseals Huawei charges and seeks Meng extradition; White House says it is a separate process from trade talks.
US soybean sales to China down 94% from the prior harvest after China’s retaliatory tariff; beans piling up in the farm belt.
China 25% soy tariff; >half of 2017 US soy exports went to China (~$12B); USDA trade-aid package up to $12B; ASA extreme disappointment at escalation/retaliation cycle.
